analysis.one_liner: Locks in lower income tax rates, repeals the estate tax, and cuts the corporate rate to 25%.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on December 15, 2010, received no hearing or vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make permanent the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts, including the lower income tax rates, the reduced tax rates on dividends and capital gains, and the full repeal of the estate and gift taxes. It would also permanently raise the exemption for the alternative minimum tax so more middle- and upper-middle-income households avoid it, and cut the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 25%, including for law, accounting, and consulting firms. It was introduced in the final weeks of the 111th Congress by Rep. Michele Bachmann and nine Republican co-sponsors and never received a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and investors gain the most, because the lower tax rates on dividends and capital gains and the repeal of the estate tax (which applies only to very large estates) become permanent. Corporations, including personal service corporations such as law and accounting firms, gain from the 25% maximum corporate rate. Middle- and upper-middle-income families also gain from permanent alternative minimum tax relief, which prevents those families from owing a parallel tax designed for the wealthy.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the 2001 tax cuts (EGTRRA) and the 2003 cuts to dividend and capital gains tax rates permanent, so they cannot expire or lapse [S2][S3].
Repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax permanently for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2010 [S2][S3].

Permanently raises the alternative minimum tax exemption (starting at $72,450 for joint filers in 2010 and rising to $109,950 by 2020), sparing many middle- and upper-middle-income households a tax originally aimed at the wealthy [S3].
Reduces the maximum corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25%, including for personal service corporations [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government: making all of these cuts permanent reduces the revenue that pays for federal programs, and the largest reductions flow to high earners, investors, large estates, and corporations. Lower revenues ultimately mean higher deficits, other tax increases, or spending cuts borne by a broader base of taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal treasury and future taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The estate tax repeal applies to the transfer of very large estates, so its benefits go exclusively to heirs of multimillion-dollar estates [S2][S3].
The 25% corporate rate applies across the board, including to personal service corporations such as law, accounting, and consulting firms, whose partners are typically high earners [S3].

Making the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent, rather than extending them temporarily, greatly increases their long-term cost to the Treasury, because the lower rates on ordinary income, dividends, and capital gains never expire [S2].
The bill contains no offsetting revenue or spending provisions, so the entire cost of the tax cuts is added to the deficit [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains one genuinely broad middle-class benefit: permanent alternative minimum tax relief, which stopped an annual legislative scramble over a tax that was hitting more ordinary families than intended. But the package is heavily weighted toward the top: permanent lock-in of low rates on investment income, full repeal of a tax on the largest estates, and a 10-point cut in the corporate rate, all without offsets. An honest supporter would acknowledge that most of the money goes to high earners, large estates, and corporations, and that the cost to federal revenue is the largest part of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2010 during the closing weeks of the 111th Congress, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and died there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote when the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Michele Bachmann introduced the bill on December 15, 2010, with nine Republican co-sponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
The full action history shows no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

At the same time, a separate compromise extending the 2001-2003 tax cuts for two years was moving through Congress and became law in December 2010, so the question of the tax cuts was resolved through that deal rather than this bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the narrow sense, ordinary taxpayers came out better than they would have under the bill, because a large package of permanent tax cuts skewed toward high earners, large estates, and corporations never became law. In the broader sense, the December 2010 tax compromise, not this bill, decided what actually happened to the tax cuts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday taxpayers; the package never passed

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means

against.what_they_did: Pursued a separate compromise in December 2010 to extend the 2001-2003 tax cuts for two years rather than make them permanent, resolving the issue outside this bill

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and co-sponsors were House Republicans, and no vote was ever taken in the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee or on the House floor.

industries.note: The bill cuts the maximum corporate rate from 35% to 25%, a broad reduction in corporate tax payments including for law, accounting, and consulting firms. Because the bill includes no offsets, the revenue the corporations no longer pay would be added to federal deficits, a cost borne by the broader taxpayer base.

Permanent repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax benefits only heirs of very large estates, and making the low dividend and capital gains rates permanent locks in tax benefits concentrated among high-income investors. The cost is reduced federal revenue available for everyone else.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt and middle-class households affected by the AMT
industries.note: The permanent alternative minimum tax exemption increase (from $72,450 in 2010 to $109,950 by 2020 for joint filers) protects many middle- and upper-middle-income families from a tax originally aimed at the wealthy. This is the bill's clearest broad-based benefit, though it also adds to the revenue cost.
